justification: Technical round 1 for /csharp-dotnet/value-types-vs-reference-types/, judged against the two top-ranking pages for 'value type vs reference type c#' (both opened and read in full). Both comparison pages state the stack/heap distinction as an unqualified rule, cite no primary sources at all, and cover none of: boxing-cost measurements, GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread, escape analysis / stack allocation in modern .NET, ref/out/in/ref-readonly, readonly struct, record struct defaults, or defensive copies (CS1612 and the three uncaught cases). This article covers all of that, with every non-obvious claim traced to a primary source I fetched and read myself: learn.microsoft.com/.../value-types, struct, ref-struct, method-parameters, record, boxing-and-unboxing, cs1612, choosing-between-class-and-struct (confirmed as a 2008-book reprint carrying its own out-of-date notice, correctly flagged by the article), the .NET 9 and .NET 10 runtime release notes (confirmed the closure-class and escape-analysis quotes verbatim, including the .NET 10 delegate/local-struct-field escape analysis the article leans on), and Eric Lippert's 'The Stack Is An Implementation Detail, Part One' (confirmed his actual thesis - value types are defined by copy-by-value semantics, storage is an implementation detail the runtime is free to choose - matches how the article uses him, not just cites him). Every direct quotation in the article (the readonly-instance-members defensive-copy sentence, 'we recommend you define immutable structure types', the ValueType.Equals 'relies on reflection' sentence, the record-struct init-only-vs-read-write default, the ref-struct boxing restrictions, the 16-byte/immutable/small/not-boxed-frequently struct criteria, and the 'int is no larger than a reference' remark) was checked word-for-word against the live page and is accurate. I re-derived the byte-count claims independently from CLR object layout (16-byte header + payload, rounded to 8) rather than trusting the article's arithmetic, and they all check out exactly: KeptObject 24 B (16 + 4 int, padded), StructArray 4,024 B (24-byte array header + 1,000x4), ClassArray 32,024 B (8,024-byte reference array + 1,000x24-byte objects), one boxed int 24 B, interpolated string 32 B vs string.Format 56 B (32 + one 24-byte box), and the plain-struct Equals cost of 48 B (two boxes: 'this' boxed by the constrained callvirt plus the object argument), against 0 B for both the hand-written IEquatable<T> struct and the record struct. That every number matches CLR layout exactly, and that `node tools/run-code.mjs` re-ran the programs on this machine and diffed their literal (non-wildcarded) output byte-for-byte, rules out fabrication. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/csharp-dotnet/value-types-vs-reference-types.md` from PowerShell: PASS, blocks=34 executed=19. I read every program in the article, including the two exercises' solutions and the CS1612/CS8852/InvalidCastException negative examples, and found no correctness or idiom problems: primary constructors, collection expressions, `[CallerArgumentExpression]`, `NoInlining`/`AggressiveOptimization`, and the generic-constraint-vs-interface comparison are all used correctly and explained precisely (worst/expected case wording is not needed here since nothing is a complexity claim, but every performance number is qualified as 'on this machine' or 'this runtime version' per the brief). Absolute wording ('every array is a reference type', 'a value-type variable always holds a value') is correctly scoped to what is actually definitional in the type system, with the one apparent overstatement - 'every ordinary type in C# converts to object' - immediately and correctly carved out for ref struct in the next paragraph. This is not a 10 only because a handful of the more obscure claims (the exact delegate-object field layout behind the 88 B closure figure, and whether every single measurement is free of tiered-JIT noise beyond the stated warm-up run) rest on the harness's exact-match verification rather than something I could independently re-derive byte-by-byte the way I did for the array and boxing figures; nothing found rises to a documented error.
